entries.narration: Syndica Bank keeps its customers' balances in a spreadsheet on a shared drive, and the head of engineering has asked the DB team a fair question: why replace it? Here is the answer, told as one morning in the Leeds branch. At nine o'clock, teller A opens the file. Olivia Bennett has five hundred pounds. A minute later, teller B opens the same file, and sees the same five hundred. Teller A pays Olivia two hundred pounds in cash, types three hundred, and saves. Then teller B pays her fifty, types four hundred and fifty, and saves. The file now says four hundred and fifty. Olivia really has two hundred and fifty. Two hundred pounds have vanished, and nothing anywhere says so. That is a lost update, and it is only the first problem. The file cannot refuse anything: type five hundred as words into a number column and it is accepted. It cannot remember who changed a balance, or why. And anyone who can open it can read every customer. A database answers each of these. Transactions let two tellers work at once and count both withdrawals. Constraints refuse bad data at the door. A ledger keeps every movement instead of overwriting a number. And access control gives each role only what it needs. This course is the DB team building exactly that, one decision at a time.

Here is the whole project, as a map. Each stage is one part of the course, and each one starts with a request from someone at the bank. First contact is this part: a server, a database, and the tool the team talks to it with. Then design: product explains that customers hold accounts, some of them jointly, and the team turns that into tables. Then build, where the database learns to refuse bad data by itself. With the bank's opening data loaded, finance starts asking questions: balances per branch, which customers hold which accounts, monthly statements and trends. Those are three stages, query, combine and analyse. Operations then needs to change data safely: interest, account closures, a nightly file from the card network. Then an incident report arrives, a customer who withdrew the same five hundred pounds twice, and the team learns transactions and concurrency properly. Site reliability reports that the statement page takes four seconds, and performance is measured, not guessed. Finally, audit finds that tellers can see every branch's customers, and access is locked down before go-live. The three green stages are this first part. Everything after them happens in the same database, which keeps every change the team makes, from the first table to the last permission. Nothing is rebuilt between stages.

Before any SQL, the shape of the system. PostgreSQL is a server: one program that owns the bank's data. It runs all the time, and it is the only thing that ever reads or writes the data files on disk. Everything else is a client. In a branch, the teller app is a client. The ATM network is a client. And the DB team's own client is psql, a program that runs in a terminal. A client sends the server text in a language called SQL; the server checks it, works out how to run it, runs it, and sends back rows or an error. One server can hold several databases. This one holds syndica, the bank's database, which is what this whole course builds, and postgres, a default the server creates for itself. On the right is a real connection. In the terminal, the team types psql, dash d, syndica. psql prints its own version and a hint, then a prompt with the database's name. The first question asks the server who we are and where: the user is dbteam, the database syndica. The second asks for the server's version: eighteen point six. Notice who answered. psql only carried the question and printed the reply. Every answer came from the server. Keep that split in mind, because some commands are answered by psql alone, and the next sections show which.

Syndica has three branches, and they make the first table. The file in the editor holds four statements, and the team runs all of it with backslash i, which tells psql to read a file and send each statement to the server. The first statement, create schema ref, makes a namespace: a named place to keep tables, here for reference data such as branches. The second creates the table itself. A table is a promise about shape. Branches has three columns, code, city and opened on, and each column has a type: code and city are text, opened on is a date. The table starts empty. The third statement inserts three rows, one per branch, with values listed in the same order as the columns. The server answers insert zero three: three rows added. And the fourth statement, select star from ref dot branches, reads every row back. The diagram on the right follows the four statements, and the table under it is exactly what the server returned: Leeds, opened in two thousand and nine, Bristol and Manchester. Notice what this table does not do yet. Nothing stops a second row for Leeds, or a branch with no city at all. A table with types but no rules accepts almost anything. The team will come back to this very table in the build stage and give it rules.

Every SQL statement is built from the same few kinds of pieces, and knowing them makes errors much easier to read. The file asks which branches opened before twenty fifteen. Select, from and where are keywords: the grammar of the language. Code, city and opened on are identifiers: the names of columns. Ref dot branches is an identifier too, a schema and a table, joined by a dot. The less-than sign is an operator. Twenty fifteen, January the first, in single quotes, is a literal: a value written directly into the statement. The semicolon ends the statement. And everything after two dashes is a comment, which the server ignores; it is there for people. Run it, and the server returns two branches, Leeds and Bristol. Manchester opened in twenty fifteen, so it is not before it. Now one detail that catches everyone. Unquoted names are folded to lower case, so city, all capitals, and city with a capital C all mean the same column. But a name in double quotes is taken exactly as written. The second statement asks for City, with a capital C, in double quotes, and the server refuses: column City does not exist. Double quotes are for names; single quotes are for values. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in SQL.

psql is more than a window onto the server. Commands that start with a backslash are psql's own, and the server never sees them as typed. Backslash d, ref dot branches, describes the table: its three columns, their types, and two columns that matter later, nullable and default, both empty for now. psql answers backslash d by sending the server ordinary queries about its catalogue, the server's own record of every table, and printing the result neatly. Backslash q quits, backslash i runs a file. Everything else you type is SQL, sent to the server as it is. The prompt is worth reading, because it tells you the state you are in. Equals, greater than, means ready for a new statement. A dash means the statement goes on to the next line. A bracket or a quote in that place means you are inside one. Now the team types begin. The server starts a transaction, and the prompt changes: there is a star in it now. Inside the transaction, they insert a branch in York. The server says insert zero one. Then they type rollback, and the star goes away. The insert has been undone completely, as if York had never been added. A star in the prompt means work that is not yet permanent. An exclamation mark would mean the transaction has failed.

Errors are how the server talks back, and the first two are worth slowing down for, because one is loud and one is silent. The team asks for the city of branch LDS, but the closing quote lands in the wrong place, before the semicolon. psql does not complain. The prompt changes to a single quote: psql is waiting for the string to end. They type the missing quote and a semicolon on the next line, the statement runs, and the answer is zero rows. No error at all. The string the server compared against was LDS, a semicolon and a line break, and no branch has that code. A wrong answer with no warning is the most dangerous kind, and the prompt was the only clue. The second mistake is loud. The team misspells city, with two t's. The server refuses, and the message has a shape worth learning. Error says the statement was refused and nothing changed. Line one shows where it stopped, and the caret points to the spot. Hint is the server's best guess: perhaps you meant branches dot city. And every error also carries a five-character code, its SQLSTATE. psql keeps the last one, and here it is four two seven zero three, undefined column. People read the message; programs check the code. That is first contact done. Next, the team designs the bank.

Product sends the team a brief. Customers open accounts at a branch. An account may be held jointly by two customers. Every deposit, card payment, transfer, fee and interest payment moves money between accounts, and each must be traceable for years. Design starts by reading for nouns, because the nouns are candidates for entities: things the bank needs to keep facts about, each of which will become a table. Customer is one. Account is another. Branch is a third. Then there is a list of movements: deposits, payments, transfers, fees. The team's decision is that these are one entity, not five. They are all the same thing, money moving between accounts, with a kind that says which. Call it a transaction. One noun is deliberately not an entity: balance. It sounds like a fact to store, but a balance is the result of every movement on an account. Store it as well, and sooner or later the stored number and the movements disagree, which is exactly how the spreadsheet lost two hundred pounds. So the balance will be calculated, never kept. On the right, each entity gets its attributes: a customer has a name, an email, a phone, and whether their identity has been checked. An account has a number, a kind, a currency, an overdraft limit, and the dates it opened and closed.

Entities are connected, and how many of one can belong to one of the other decides where the connection is stored. A branch has many accounts, but an account belongs to one branch. That is one to many, and it is stored as a column on the many side: each account row names its branch. A transaction has many postings, and each posting belongs to one transaction: one to many again, a column in postings. Customers and accounts are different. Chloe Price holds two accounts, and her current account is held jointly with Marcus Reid. So one customer has many accounts, and one account has many customers. That is many to many, and no single column can hold it: an account row cannot list two customers without repeating itself. The answer is a table of its own, account holders. Each row pairs one account with one customer, and points at both. The table on the right shows it with real data from the bank: account ending one three appears twice, once for Chloe and once for Marcus, and Chloe appears twice, once for each of her accounts. Nothing else about Chloe or the account is repeated, only the pairing. That small table is what makes joint accounts possible, and it will matter again later, when adding up balances per customer suddenly counts a joint account twice.

Every row needs a name: something that picks out exactly one row and never changes. That name is the primary key, and choosing it is one of the most important design decisions. Take accounts. The obvious candidate is the account number, printed on every card and statement. It is unique, but it is not stable: when a card is compromised, the bank reissues the account under a new number. If every posting had used the account number to say which account it belongs to, a reissue would mean rewriting every one of them. Branch plus opening date is not even unique, since two accounts can open on the same day. So the team uses a surrogate key: account ID, a number the database hands out, which means nothing at all. Because it means nothing, there is never a reason to change it. Account one zero one three stays one zero one three for ever. The account number is still kept, and declared unique, because people read it, print it and type it. It is looked up once, and from then on everything points at the account ID. The same test applied to customers gives the same answer. A name is not unique: the bank will soon have two Priya Shahs. An email is unique but changes. So customers get a customer ID too, with email kept unique.

The legacy system kept accounts in one wide sheet, one row per holder per account, with the holder's email and the branch city written on every row. To see why that design fails, the team rebuilds it in a schema called sandbox, a throwaway that will be dropped at the end. Chloe Price holds two accounts, so her email appears on two rows. Now she changes her email address, and someone updates her savings account row. The server reports update one: exactly one row changed, as asked. Then the team asks the sheet for Chloe's email, and gets two different answers, one per row. Nothing was rejected and nothing crashed; the data simply contradicts itself. That is an update anomaly, and it is one of three. An insert anomaly: a new customer with no account yet has nowhere to go, because a row needs an account. A delete anomaly: close Chloe's last account, and Chloe herself disappears. All three come from the same cause: a fact stored in more than one place. Normalisation is the discipline of storing each fact once. Chloe's email lives in one customers row, and the pairing of customers to accounts lives in account holders, which only points at her. Change the email once, and every account sees the change. Then the team drops the sandbox schema, and with it the sheet.

Banks have recorded money the same way for centuries, and the design follows that method, called double entry. Money is never created or destroyed; it moves from one account to another, and every movement is written twice: once leaving, once arriving. Each of those lines is a posting. When Olivia pays Hassan one hundred and fifty pounds, that is one transaction with two postings: minus one fifty on Olivia's account, plus one fifty on Hassan's. When Tom is charged a fifteen pound fee, the money does not disappear: it moves from Tom's account to the bank's own fee income account, minus fifteen and plus fifteen. The bank keeps internal accounts like that for fees, interest, card settlement, and money arriving from outside, so that every pound has somewhere to come from and somewhere to go. Three rules follow. A transaction's postings always sum to zero. A balance is the sum of an account's postings, never a number someone edits. And a mistake is never fixed by changing history, only by a new transaction that reverses it. On the right, the same four postings are written as a query over a list of values, and the server prints them back. Then it adds up the amounts: zero point zero zero. That sum, always zero, is the ledger's built-in check.

Before anything is built, the design is reviewed, and the last questions are about types: what kind of value each column holds. Money first. Asked to add zero point one and zero point two as float eight, a binary floating point number, the server answers zero point three, followed by a long tail of digits ending in four. Binary floating point cannot store a tenth exactly, and in a bank those tiny errors add up across millions of postings. Numeric stores decimals exactly, and the same sum is exactly zero point three. So every amount is numeric fourteen comma two: up to fourteen digits, two of them after the point. The second query shows what the two means: ten point zero zero five is stored as ten point zero one, rounded the way a bank would round it. Dates are simpler. A day an account opened is a date, with no time and no time zone. But the moment a transaction is booked is a timestamp with time zone: one instant in time, which the server can show in any zone. Here it is nine in the morning on the thirty-first of October. On the left is version one of the schema, signed off: customers, account holders, accounts, branches, transactions and postings. Every arrow is a reference by surrogate key. The next stage builds it, and makes it refuse bad data.

The build begins with customers. The file creates a schema called core, for the bank's main tables, and a customers table inside it. Two columns are filled by the database rather than by whoever inserts a row. Customer ID is generated always as identity: the database numbers customers itself, one after another, so nobody has to choose a number or worry about clashing with someone else's. KYC status, short for know your customer, has a default of pending: every new customer starts unverified until their identity has been checked. In the terminal, the team inserts the first two customers, Amelia Hughes and Daniel Okafor, giving only their name, email, phone and joining date. The statement ends with returning, which asks the server to send back columns of the rows it just inserted. And there they are: customer one and customer two, both pending. The database chose the IDs and applied the default. Then the team tries to insert a customer with an ID of seven, chosen by hand. The server refuses, and the detail explains why: the column is an identity column, generated always. The hint even names the way around it, overriding system value, which exists for loading data that already has IDs. The team will need exactly that idea when the bank's opening data is loaded, later in this stage.

The branches table from the first stage has no key, and the team shows what that costs. Someone registers Leeds again, with today's date. The server accepts it: insert zero one. There are now two rows for Leeds, and no rule says that is wrong. So the team adds the rule: alter table ref dot branches, add primary key code. The server refuses, and the detail says why: key code equals LDS is duplicated. A constraint is checked against the rows already in the table, not just future ones, and this table already breaks it. The duplicate must go first. Notice how it is removed: the delete names the code and the opening date, because without a key, those values are the only way to point at one of the two rows. The server reports delete one, exactly one row, which is the number to check every time anything is deleted. Then the keys file runs: a primary key on branches, a primary key on customers, and a unique constraint on customer email, so two customers can never share one. Finally, the team tries to register Leeds a second time, and now the server refuses: key code equals LDS already exists. A primary key is two promises at once: every row has a value, and no two rows share it. Unique on its own allows a missing value.

Accounts come next, and they refer to other tables. An account's branch code references ref dot branches: a foreign key, which means every branch code in accounts must exist in branches. Account holders is the joint-account table from the design. Each of its columns references a table, accounts and customers, and its primary key is both columns together, a composite key, so the same customer can never be added to the same account twice. In the terminal, the team tries to open an account at branch YRK. There is no York branch, so the server refuses: key branch code equals YRK is not present in table branches. Then the same account at Leeds succeeds. The guard works in the other direction too. The team tries to delete the Leeds branch, and the server refuses again, because an account still references it. That is the on delete restrict in the file, and it was a deliberate choice. Cascade would have deleted Leeds's accounts along with the branch; set null would have left them with no branch at all. For anything that holds money, refusing is the only safe answer. One detail for later: the refused York insert still used up identity number one, so Amelia's new account is number two. Identity numbers are never handed out twice, and gaps are normal.

Now the rules every row must obey. Not null says a column must always have a value: a customer must have a name, an account a number, a kind, a branch and an opening date. Check says a value must pass a test: an account's kind is current, savings or internal; its currency is pounds or euros; its overdraft limit is never negative; and it cannot close before it opened. Every one of these is added to a table that already has rows, so the server tests the existing data as it adds each rule. Here all of it passes. Now look at the one account so far. Its closed on column is NULL, which means no value at all, and in this column that means the account is still open. That is how NULL should be read: column by column. A NULL phone means not given; a NULL name is now forbidden. And here is the subtle part. Checking that closed on is on or after opened on, with closed on NULL, is neither true nor false. It is unknown. A check constraint only refuses a row when its test is false, so unknown passes, and open accounts are accepted. Then the team tries to close the account on the thirty-first of August, before it opened. That test is false, and the server refuses: the row violates the check constraint.

Time to test the rules, and to test yourself. The file holds six records, each with a comment saying what it is. Before the result, pause and predict each one: accepted, or refused, and by which rule. Number one is a customer with no phone. Number two, a customer with no name. Three is Amelia again, with the same email. Four, an account in dollars. Five, an account that closes before it opens. And six, Priya Shah, joining with her email p dot shah. The file starts with backslash set verbosity terse, which makes psql print each error on one line. Here are the verdicts. One is accepted: phone may be NULL. Two is refused by not null on full name. Three is refused by the unique constraint on email. Four is refused by the check on currency. Five is refused by the check on the dates. And six is accepted. Each refused row was stopped by a rule written once, in the schema, that no application can forget. But look again at number six. The bank's opening data, loaded next, already contains Priya Shah, under the email priya dot shah. Two emails, so nothing unique is broken, yet it is the same person twice. Constraints guard each row; spotting duplicates needs a query, and that is a job for the change stage.

The schema is ready for real data, and two tables are still missing: the ledger. Transactions records each movement of money, with a kind, a reference, and the instant it was booked. Postings records the lines of each transaction, every amount numeric, never zero. Then the opening book: five files of customers, accounts, account holders, transactions and postings, loaded with backslash copy, which reads a file on the team's machine and streams it to the server. Order matters. The team first tries to load postings on their own, and the server refuses: key transaction ID five zero zero one is not present in transactions. A posting can only refer to a transaction that already exists. So the load file goes parents first: customers, then accounts, then the holders that link them, then transactions, then postings. The server counts each one: ten customers, fifteen accounts, twelve holder pairs, thirty-six transactions and seventy-two postings, two for every transaction. The files carry their own IDs, starting at one hundred and one for customers, so they never meet the rows the team created by hand. But copy writes those IDs without moving the identity counter, which is still near the start. Left alone, some future insert would try to create customer one hundred and one again. So the last four statements move each identity past the loaded rows.

The server keeps a record of everything the team has created: every schema, table, column, type and constraint. That record is the catalogue, and the database describes itself through it. Backslash dt, core dot star, is psql's shortcut for listing tables, and it shows the five tables in core, all owned by dbteam. The same facts are available in plain SQL, through information schema, a set of views defined by the SQL standard, so the query works on other databases too. Here the team asks for the columns of postings, with their types and whether each may be null. Four columns, all bigint or numeric, and none of them nullable. The editor shows where those answers came from: the create table statement in the ledger file. The catalogue is what tools use to draw diagrams, what migration tools compare, and what an auditor reads to see exactly what the database enforces. With that, the build is complete. Syndica Bank now has branches, customers, accounts and their holders, and a double-entry ledger, with keys, references and rules the database enforces on every row, and its opening book loaded and counted. Nothing has been asked of the data yet. Next, finance has questions, and the team starts querying.

The bank is open, and finance has questions. Every answer starts with select: which columns, from which table. The first question looks simple: what kinds of account does each branch offer? Counting the accounts table first, the server says sixteen rows, one per account. But finance did not ask about accounts; they asked about branches and kinds. Select distinct branch code and kind returns six rows, one for each combination that exists: Bristol offers current and savings accounts, Leeds current accounts and the bank's internal ones, Manchester current and savings. Distinct removes duplicate rows from the answer, and in doing so it changes what one row means. This idea has a name, the grain of a result: what a single row stands for. In the accounts table, one row is one account. In this answer, one row is one combination of branch and kind. Before reading any answer, say its grain out loud, because most wrong reports are correct numbers at the wrong grain: a total per account read as a total per customer, or a count of rows read as a count of people. The query also renames its columns with as, so branch code comes back as branch, and it sorts the result, which gets its own section shortly.

Where keeps the rows that pass a test and drops the rest. Finance asks for the transactions booked on the second and third of October. The obvious way to write that is between: booked at between the second and the third. The server returns two transactions, both on the second. But there are three. Transaction five zero two zero, the loan being repaid, was booked at quarter to five in the afternoon of the third, and between missed it. The reason is in the type. Booked at is a timestamp, a moment in time, and a date written with no time means midnight at its start. So between the second and the third means from midnight on the second up to midnight on the third, and nothing later on the third is included. The fix is a half-open range: on or after midnight on the second, and strictly before midnight on the fourth. That form is always right for timestamps, whatever the precision, and it returns all three. Two more shorthands are worth knowing. In tests against a list: kind in card, fee means kind equals card or kind equals fee. Like matches a pattern, where percent stands for any text, so reference like CAFE percent finds every reference starting with café. Together, they find four café transactions.

Some customers have no phone on file, and finance wants to know who. The first attempt asks for phone equals null, and the server returns zero rows. Not an error, just nothing. The reason is that NULL is not a value; it means no value is known. Asking whether an unknown phone equals an unknown is itself unknown, and where only keeps rows whose test is true. So phone equals null is never true, for any row, and SQL quietly returns nothing. This is three-valued logic: a test can be true, false, or unknown. The right question is phone is null, which is always true or false. It finds four customers: Grace Lin and Priya Shah, both added by hand in the build stage, and Chloe Price and Tom Walsh from the opening data. The trap has a second form that is easier to miss. Finance asks how many customers have a phone number other than Olivia's, and the answer is nine. There are fourteen customers. Olivia is one; the other four are missing because their phone is NULL, and comparing NULL with Olivia's number is unknown, so those rows were dropped too. When a column can be NULL, every comparison on it has three outcomes, and the question is always: what should happen to the unknowns?

A select can compute values, not only read them. The first query shows four small rules. Seven divided by two gives three, because both numbers are integers and integer division drops the fraction. Make either side a decimal, seven divided by two point zero, and the answer is exactly three and a half. Round two point six seven five to two places, and numeric gives two point six eight: decimal arithmetic rounds the way people expect, which binary floating point would not. And the text forty-two, cast with two colons to an integer, becomes a number you can add one to. Casts convert between types, and they fail loudly if the text is not a number. The file then answers a real question: for each current account with an overdraft, what would a full overdraft cost a month at nineteen point nine percent a year? The account number is masked for a report that leaves the bank: six stars, then the right four characters, joined with two vertical bars, which is SQL's operator for joining text. The cost is the limit times the rate divided by twelve, rounded to pence. And date trunc rounds the opening date down to the first of its month. Every column of a result can be an expression like these, computed fresh for each row.

Finance wants each overdraft placed in a tier: none, small, or large. Case is SQL's way to choose a value by testing conditions. It lists when-then branches and an optional else, and it tests them in order, top to bottom. The first branch whose test is true decides the result, and the rest are never looked at. In the file, a limit of zero is none, under two hundred and fifty is small, and anything else is large. The result is right: Hassan's account with no overdraft is none, Tom's one hundred is small, and the two at two fifty and five hundred are large. Now the same two tests, written in the other order: under two hundred and fifty first, then equals zero. Asked about Hassan's account, the server says small. Zero is less than two hundred and fifty, so the first branch matched, and the branch for zero was never reached. Nothing warned anyone. The rule for writing case is to go from the most specific test to the most general, and to remember that ranges overlap unless you make them not overlap. A case with no else, and no branch that matches, returns NULL, which is one more reason to write the else even when you think every case is covered.

Tom wants his statement online, three lines a page. A table has no order of its own: rows come back in whatever order is cheapest for the server, and that order can change from one day to the next. Only order by guarantees an order, and only if what it sorts by is unique. Sort postings by amount, and two postings of the same amount can swap places between two requests, so a line could appear on both pages or on neither. Sorting by posting ID, which is unique, gives one fixed order. Limit three then returns the first page: Tom's opening deposit, an ATM withdrawal, and a payment at a garage. For page two there are two methods. Offset three skips the first three rows and returns the next three. It works, but the server still reads and throws away every row before the page, so page five hundred reads one thousand five hundred rows to show three. And if a posting is added while Tom reads, every later page shifts by one. The second method, keyset paging, remembers where page one ended, posting nine zero four one, and asks for postings after it. It starts exactly where the last page stopped, does the same work for page five hundred as for page two, and nothing Tom has already seen moves.

Finance's first real report: the balance of every account. The design said a balance is never stored, and here is why that works. An aggregate function turns many rows into one value: sum adds them, count counts them, and min, max and avg do what their names say. Group by decides which rows are aggregated together, here every posting of the same account. So each output row is one account, with the number of postings it has and their sum, which is its balance. Olivia has two thousand two hundred and ninety-eight pounds ninety-five. Tom, whose account dipped below zero in October, has two hundred and eighty-nine fifty today. Ben's closed account sums to exactly zero, as a closed account should. The where clause drops the bank's internal accounts before grouping. Notice one account is missing: Amelia's, opened by hand in the build stage. It has no postings, so it has no rows to group, and it is simply not in the answer. A later stage finds it again. The last query shows a difference that catches everyone. Count star counts rows: fourteen customers. Count phone counts values: ten. Count of a column skips NULLs, so the two counts differ by exactly the four customers with no phone.

SQL is written in one order and evaluated in another, and knowing the second order explains a whole family of errors. A query is written select first. But logically, the server starts with from: every row of the table. Then where keeps or drops each individual row. Only then does group by turn rows into groups, and having keeps or drops whole groups. Select computes the output columns after that, and order by and limit come last. The team asks which accounts have a negative balance, and first writes sum of amount less than zero in the where clause. The server refuses: aggregate functions are not allowed in where. Of course: at the moment where runs, there are no groups yet, and so no sums. Moved to having, the question works, and the answer is two internal accounts. External clearing is minus sixteen thousand four hundred and eighty, which is all the money that has come into the bank from outside. Interest paid is minus nine pounds six. The third query is the real trap, because it runs without error. Filtering amount less than zero in where, then summing, adds up only the money going out, so every account looks negative. A filter on rows and a filter on groups answer different questions. Next, finance needs answers that span several tables.

Finance's next questions span more than one table. Which city is each account in? The account knows only its branch code; the city lives in branches. A join puts the two together. It pairs each row of one table with the rows of another that satisfy a condition, here branches dot code equals accounts dot branch code. The tables get short aliases, a and b, so every column can say which table it comes from. The file asks for every Manchester account with its city, and gets four: Chloe and Marcus's joint current account, Chloe's savings, Ben's closed account, and Liam's. This is an inner join, the default kind: a pair appears only when the condition matches, and a row with no partner disappears. Before trusting any join, check its grain, just as with a single table. Every account has exactly one branch, so joining accounts to branches should give one row per account, no more and no fewer. The second query proves it: sixteen rows, the same as accounts on its own. When a join returns more rows than you expected, something on the other side matched more than once, and when it returns fewer, something did not match at all. The next two sections are about exactly those two cases.

An inner join drops rows with no match. Sometimes those rows are the answer. Which customers hold no account at all? A left join keeps every row of the left table, customers, and where nothing in account holders matches, it fills the holder's columns with NULL. So asking for rows where the holder's account ID is null finds exactly the customers with no match. There are three. Grace Lin and Priya Shah were added by hand in the build stage. And Amelia Hughes, the very first customer, holds nothing, because the account opened for her during the build never got a row in account holders. An outer join just found a real gap in the data, which the change stage will fix. Now the most common outer join mistake. The team wants every customer, together with any accounts numbered above one zero one five. Put that condition in the on clause, and all fourteen customers come back: the condition decides which holder rows match, and unmatched customers stay, with NULLs. Put the same condition in where, and only six come back. Where runs after the join, and for a customer with no matching holder the account ID is NULL, so NULL greater than one zero one five is unknown and the row is dropped. The outer join has quietly become an inner join.

A transfer is one transaction with two postings: one leg leaving an account, one leg arriving. To list transfers as from this account to that one, both legs have to sit on the same output row, and both live in the same table. So the query joins postings to itself. It names the table twice, with two aliases: out, for the leg whose amount is negative, and inn, for the leg whose amount is positive. Each alias is joined to the transaction by its ID, so the two legs of the same transaction pair up. Aliases are what make this possible: without them, the server could not tell which copy of postings a column belongs to. The answer is four transfers. Rent share from Olivia's account to Hassan's. A loan from Hassan to Aisha. The loan repaid, from Aisha back to Olivia. And Chloe moving five hundred pounds from her current account to her savings. Read the first three again: one zero one one to one zero one two, one zero one two to one zero one nine, one zero one nine back to one zero one one. The same one hundred and fifty pounds went round in a circle in two days. A self-join finds one step of a chain; following a chain of any length needs a recursive query, which is where the analyse stage begins.

Finance asks how much money each customer holds, and the obvious query joins customers to account holders to postings and sums per customer. For Chloe and Marcus it returns seven thousand eight hundred and twelve pounds fifty-one for Chloe, and two thousand three hundred and three forty-five for Marcus. Each figure is defensible on its own: Chloe can spend everything in her savings and the joint account, and so can Marcus in the joint account. But now add up money held across all customers. Through accounts, the bank holds fifteen thousand six hundred and sixty-six pounds eighty-seven. Through customers, the same postings add up to seventeen thousand nine hundred and seventy pounds thirty-two. The difference is two thousand three hundred and three forty-five, exactly the balance of the joint account. Each of its postings met two holder rows in the join, so it was counted once for Chloe and once for Marcus. This is duplicate amplification: a join that fans out, one row on one side meeting several on the other, multiplies every value carried along with it, and a sum or count after it is silently too big. Nothing errors. The defence is the grain question again: after each join, what does one row mean? Here, one row is a posting per holder, not a posting.

A subquery is a query inside another, in brackets, and where it sits decides what it must return. In where, it can be scalar: one value. The first statement compares each account's balance with the average amount of all money coming in, a single number the inner query computes once. In from, a subquery is a derived table: the inner query groups postings into balances, and the outer query treats that result as a table called b. Top three: Chloe's savings, the joint account, and Olivia's. The file shows the third kind, which is the most powerful. A correlated subquery refers to the outer query's current row, so it runs again for each row. Finance wants each account's two latest postings. The subquery picks postings for one account, newest first, limit two, and lateral is what allows it to use a dot account ID from outside. For Olivia's account, the latest two are a greengrocer payment and the loan repaid; for Tom's, two café payments. Top N per group is a very common question, and lateral answers it directly. A correlated subquery is not free, though: it runs once per outer row. On sixteen accounts that is nothing; on sixteen million it is a decision, and the performance stage measures that kind of decision.

Which transactions have never been reversed? The natural way to write it: transaction ID not in the list of reverses values. The server answers zero. Every transaction reversed? That cannot be right, and the second query shows why. Of thirty-six transactions, only one has a value in reverses. The other thirty-five are NULL, because they are not reversals. So the list inside not in contains thirty-five NULLs. Not in means not equal to the first value, and not equal to the second, and so on. Comparing anything with NULL is unknown, so for every transaction the whole test is unknown, never true, and no row survives. One NULL in the list empties the result. This is a classic trap, because the query looks correct and the subquery's column did not look nullable to whoever wrote it. Not exists asks a different question. For each transaction, it asks whether there exists any reversal pointing at it. Exists only cares whether a matching row is there, and a NULL never matches, so it cannot poison the answer. Thirty-five transactions were never reversed, which is the truth. The rule worth remembering: for 'not in a list from another table', use not exists, unless you are certain the column can never be NULL.

Set operators combine whole query results rather than tables. Both sides must return the same number of columns, of compatible types, and the result is one list. Union returns rows from either side. Intersect returns rows that appear on both. Except returns rows on the left that do not appear on the right. Product wants to know which customers hold a savings account but no current account, to offer them one. The file's top query lists holders of savings accounts, and the bottom one holders of current accounts. Except takes the first list minus the second. Chloe holds savings, but she also holds the joint current account, so she is removed. One customer is left: one zero seven, Sofia Rossi. One detail matters for counting. Union, intersect and except remove duplicate rows from their result, as if distinct were applied. Stack the holders list on top of itself with union, and the answer is eleven, the distinct customers who hold anything. Union all keeps every row, duplicates included, and the answer is twenty-four, twice the twelve holder rows. Union all is also cheaper, because the server does not have to look for duplicates. Use union when duplicates would be wrong, and union all when you know there are none, or want them.

Finance now asks for balances almost every day, and every one of those queries repeats the same join and sum. A view gives a query a name. The file creates core dot account balance: every account, its number and kind, and the sum of its postings, with a left join so an account with no postings still appears, and coalesce turning its missing sum into zero. The server answers create view, and from now on anyone can select from account balance as if it were a table. The three largest current balances are the joint account, Olivia's and Hassan's. A view stores the query, not the result. Every time someone reads it, the server runs the stored query, so balances are still derived from postings at that moment and can never drift out of date. That keeps the design's promise and gives everyone a short, correct way to ask. The view is also an interface: if the tables change later, the view can be redefined and the queries that use it keep working. There are limits. The team tries to set a balance to zero through the view, and the server refuses: views containing group by are not automatically updatable. Here that refusal is exactly right: a balance is a sum, and there is nothing to write it into. Next comes analysis.

Finance wants a real monthly statement for Tom: what he had on the first of October, what came in, what went out, and what he has now. As one query that would be a knot of nested subqueries. A common table expression, written with with, lets the query be built in named stages instead. The first stage, tom, gathers Tom's postings with the moment each was booked. The second, opening, adds up everything before the first of October. The third, october, adds up the month's money in and money out, using filter to sum only positive amounts in one column and only negative ones in the other. Each stage reads the ones before it by name, as if they were tables, and the final select puts them side by side. Tom opened October with one hundred and eighty pounds, paid in four hundred, paid out two hundred and ninety fifty, and closes on two hundred and eighty-nine fifty. That closing figure is the same balance the group by query found in the query stage, which is a quiet check that both are right. Stages are not only easier to read; each can be tested on its own by selecting from it. When a long query gives a surprising answer, a with clause is where you take it apart.

The self-join in the combine stage found single transfers. Risk wants more: follow money out of Olivia's account, as far as it goes. A chain of unknown length needs a recursive query. With recursive starts with an anchor, here every transfer out of account one zero one one. Then a recursive part joins the last hop found to the next transfer out of its destination, and the server repeats that until no new rows appear. Hop one: from Olivia's account to Hassan's. Hop two: Hassan to Aisha. Hop three: Aisha back to Olivia. And then a danger: from Olivia, the recursion finds hop one again, and again after that, for ever. Money that moves in a circle is exactly the pattern risk teams look for, and exactly the one that makes a naive recursive query never finish. The cycle clause, available in PostgreSQL since version fourteen, tracks the accounts visited on each path. When a row would visit one again, it is marked looped, and the recursion stops there. So the fourth row is hop one repeated, flagged true, and that is the end. Without cycle, the same protection needs a manual path array and a check; with it, a loop is a fact in the result instead of a query that never returns.

A statement needs every line, and next to each line, the balance after it. Group by cannot do that: it collapses rows into one sum. A window function computes over a set of rows, called its window, but keeps every row in the result. Sum of amount, over, order by booked at, means: for this row, sum every posting from the first one up to this one, in time order. The posting ID is a tie-breaker, so the order is fully determined. The result is Tom's whole history as a statement. He opened with a three hundred pound deposit. After an ATM withdrawal, one hundred and eighty. In October, a garage and a tyre shop take him below zero: minus fifty-five, then minus seventy after the overdraft fee. On the ninth his salary arrives and he is back to three hundred and thirty, and two café payments later he is on two hundred and eighty-nine fifty, the same balance as before. His lowest point, minus seventy, stayed inside his one hundred pound overdraft limit. The balance on each line was never stored anywhere; it was derived from postings at the moment of asking, just like every balance in this database. A window turns a rule from the design stage into a statement a customer can read.

A window's frame decides exactly which rows are summed for each row, and the default is subtler than it looks. This query runs a total over the whole ledger in time order, twice. The first uses rows unbounded preceding: every row from the start up to this physical row. The second uses range unbounded preceding, which is what you get by default when a window has an order by. The difference appears with ties. Both legs of a transaction share the same booked at moment, so in this order they are peers. Rows sums up to this exact row, so after the first leg of Olivia's salary it shows two thousand four hundred, half a transaction, and after the second leg, zero. Range includes every peer of the current row, so for both legs it sums the whole transaction at once and shows zero. Down the ledger, the range column stays at zero after every transaction, which is the double-entry rule made visible: the books balance after each movement. The rows column wobbles because it cuts transactions in half. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. The lesson is to know which frame you are getting, and to break ties with a unique column, as the running balance did, when you mean one row at a time.

Which accounts use their cards most often? Three window functions rank rows, and they differ only when there are ties. Tom's account has four card payments, first by every measure. Olivia's and the joint account have two each: a tie. Rank gives both second place and then skips, so the next account is fourth. Dense rank gives both second and continues with third, with no gap. Row number never ties: it numbers rows one, two, three, using the account ID to break the tie, so every row gets a different number. Which one to use is a business question. Top three by rank could return more than three rows; top three by row number returns exactly three, but which of two tied accounts makes the cut is arbitrary unless you choose the tie-breaker. Row number has a second job: finding duplicates. Partition by full name restarts the numbering for each name, ordered by customer ID. Any row numbered two or more shares a name with an earlier customer. There is exactly one: customer one zero five, Priya Shah, from the opening book, a second record for the Priya Shah the team added by hand in the build stage. A name match is only a suspicion, not proof; the change stage confirms it and merges the two.

Many questions compare a row with its neighbour: this month against last month, this transaction against the one before. Lag reads a value from the previous row in the window's order, and lead from the next. The file first adds up card spending per month in a with stage, then puts each month beside the one before it. September, two hundred and seventeen forty-four. October, five hundred and eighty-nine seventy-five, with September's figure as its previous value and a change of three hundred and seventy-two thirty-one. September has no previous month, so lag returns NULL there, and the change is NULL too: there is nothing to compare with, and SQL says so rather than inventing a zero. The second query measures time between Tom's transactions. For each day, the day minus the previous day gives the gap. Two days after his first deposit, a withdrawal. Then twenty-three days with nothing. Then three days running, and a two-day gap before his salary. Gaps like these are what fraud and engagement models are built on, and lag makes them one line of SQL instead of a self-join on 'the previous row', which plain SQL has no direct way to name. Both functions take an offset and a default, for when you want two rows back, or a zero instead of NULL.

Risk asks a sharper question about Tom: on which runs of consecutive days did he end the day overdrawn? Runs of consecutive values are called islands, and the gaps between them gaps, and there is a classic trick for finding them. First, the query builds a calendar: generate series makes one row for every day in October. For each day, a scalar subquery adds up Tom's postings booked before midnight at its end, giving his end-of-day balance. Then it keeps only the days below zero. Now the trick. Number those days in order, and subtract the number from the date. On consecutive days, the date goes up by one and so does the number, so the difference stays the same. The sixth minus one, the seventh minus two, and the eighth minus three are all the fifth of October. That shared value is an island's label. A gap in the days makes the date jump while the number does not, so the label changes, and a new island begins. Group by the label, and each island becomes one row with its first day, last day and length. Tom has one island: from the sixth to the eighth of October, three days, exactly as the opening data intended. The same pattern finds streaks, outages and sessions in any time series.

The last report of the analysis stage is the one every board wants: balances by branch and account kind, with a subtotal per branch and a grand total, all in one result. Group by rollup of branch and kind produces three levels of grouping at once: each branch and kind, each branch on its own, and everything. The rows where a column has been rolled up show NULL in that column, which is ambiguous if real data can be NULL, so the grouping function returns a level number saying which columns were rolled up: zero for a detail row, one for a branch subtotal, three for the grand total. Bristol holds two thousand six hundred and sixty-six pounds, Leeds four thousand nine hundred and thirty-eight thirty-six, Manchester eight thousand and sixty-two fifty-one, and the bank fifteen thousand six hundred and sixty-six eighty-seven, the same total the combine stage found through accounts. Filter adds a conditional count beside the sums: open accounts only, where closed on is NULL, so Ben's closed account is counted nowhere. Rollup is shorthand for a list of grouping sets; cube would add every combination, such as kind across all branches. That completes finance's questions. Next, operations needs to change data, safely.

Operations has tickets, and every one of them changes data for good. So before any change, the team uses one routine. Ticket one: identity checks have passed for Tom Walsh and Liam Murphy, and their KYC status must become verified. Step one: run a select with exactly the where clause the update will use, and count. Two customers, both pending, both the right people. That count is a prediction. Step two: begin a transaction, so nothing is permanent yet, and run the update. Its where clause names the two customers, and also requires their status to still be pending, so running the ticket twice changes nothing the second time. Returning prints the rows as they now are, and the server reports update two. Step three: compare. The prediction said two, the server says two, and the rows are the right ones, so the team commits. Had the server said two thousand, the answer would be rollback, and nothing would have happened at all. This is the habit that separates a safe change from a famous incident. And notice what was updated: a customer's status. In this database, some data is never updated: no update statement ever touches a posting. Money that moved stays moved, and the next sections show what happens instead when something has to be undone.

Ticket two: customer number six is Priya Shah again. The analysis stage flagged two Priya Shahs; Operations phoned her, and they are the same person. Customer one zero five holds her account, and customer six holds nothing, so customer six can go. The delete is written defensively. Inside a transaction, it names the customer, and adds a condition that no account holder row points at her, so if anything had been attached, the delete would remove nothing instead of breaking something. Returning shows exactly the record being removed: Priya Shah, p dot shah at example dot com. Delete one, as predicted, and commit. Now the other kind of request. Ben's account was closed in October; could it simply be deleted? The server refuses. The account is still referenced, first by its holder row, and behind that by every posting it ever had. That refusal is the design working. A bank must keep closed accounts and their history for years, so an account is never deleted; it is closed, by setting its closed on date, and Ben's already shows the twentieth of October. Deleting is for rows that should never have existed. Closing is for things that existed and ended, and the foreign keys make sure the database cannot confuse the two.

Ticket three fixes the gap the outer join found in the combine stage: Amelia's account, opened by hand during the build, has no holder. The fix is a single row in account holders, with Amelia's account ID and her customer ID. Operations does not know those IDs, and should not have to. They know the account number on her card and her email address. Insert select inserts the rows a query returns, instead of rows typed out in values. Here the query looks up the account by its number and the customer by her email, and returns their IDs, which become the new row. Returning shows what was inserted: account two, customer one, which is exactly where the identity numbers landed back in the build stage. Insert zero one. Typing the numbers directly would have worked too, until the day someone typed the wrong one, and a perfectly valid row linked the wrong customer to the wrong account. A mistyped email, on the other hand, matches nobody, so the select returns nothing and nothing is inserted. Running the combine stage's query again confirms the fix. The customers with no account were Amelia, Grace and the duplicate Priya. Priya is gone, Amelia now holds her account, and only Grace Lin is left, who genuinely has not opened one yet.

Ticket four: the property team sends the official branch list. Manchester's branch is now called Manchester Piccadilly, and a new branch opens in York in November. The file loads the list into a temporary table, which disappears when the session ends, and applies it with merge. Merge joins a source to a target and says what to do in each case. When a branch matches and its city differs, update the city. When a branch in the list is not in the table, insert it. Leeds matches with the same city, so nothing happens to it. Since PostgreSQL seventeen, merge can return its rows along with which action touched each one: Manchester updated, York inserted. Merge two. The second statement shows the older tool, insert with on conflict, often called an upsert. Run with the same list, it reports insert zero three. Nothing new was inserted, and nothing needed to change, but all three branches were rewritten, and the command tag cannot tell you which happened to which row. Each tool has its job. On conflict is a single atomic statement for one key, and it is the safe way to insert-or-update when two sessions might do it at once. Merge applies a whole feed with several outcomes, and reports exactly what it did. The concurrency stage revisits why that difference matters.

Ticket five: Tom is to get his fifteen pound overdraft fee back. The tempting fix is to delete the fee, or update it to zero. Either would rewrite history: Tom's October statement would change after it was sent, and the ledger would no longer show what really happened on the seventh of October. In double-entry bookkeeping a mistake is corrected by a new transaction that reverses it. The file does this in one statement, using a data-modifying CTE. The with stage inserts the reversal transaction: kind reversal, a reference saying refund, booked on the thirty-first, and reverses pointing at the fee, transaction five zero two three. It returns the new transaction's ID. The outer insert then copies every posting of the fee into the reversal with its sign flipped: plus fifteen to Tom, minus fifteen from fee income. Two postings that sum to zero, so the ledger still balances. Both transactions now sit side by side: the fee, and the reversal that names it. Tom's balance, read from the view, has risen from two hundred and eighty-nine fifty to three hundred and four fifty. Nothing was edited and nothing was deleted, and anyone reading the ledger can see the fee, the refund, and exactly when each happened.

The last ticket comes from audit: every change to a customer's details must be recorded, with what it was before, what it became, and who changed it. Relying on every application to remember that is how records go missing. So the database does it itself, with a trigger. The file creates an audit schema and a table for customer changes, with the old and new row stored as JSON. Then a function, written in PL/pgSQL, PostgreSQL's procedural language, inserts one audit row from the old and new versions of the row being changed. The trigger attaches that function to customers: after update, for each row. Now Chloe changes her email address. The team runs an ordinary update, and the server reports update one. But one statement caused two writes. The trigger fired inside the same transaction and recorded the change: customer one zero three, from chloe dot price at example dot com, to chloe at example dot org, by dbteam. If the update had rolled back, the audit row would have rolled back with it. Triggers are powerful precisely because they are invisible, which is also their cost: every update to customers now does extra work that its author cannot see, and a slow or failing trigger makes every update slow or failing. That completes Operations' tickets.

An incident report lands on the team's desk: a customer withdrew the same five hundred pounds twice. Before the incident itself, the foundations. The bank has invariants, rules that must hold after every change: every transaction's postings sum to zero, and no account goes below its overdraft limit. A transaction is how a database keeps them, and it makes four promises, known as ACID. Atomic: all of it happens, or none of it. Consistent: every rule holds when it ends. Isolated: other sessions see the world before it or after it, never halfway. Durable: once committed, it survives a crash, because it is written to the write-ahead log first. The file creates two functions the rest of this stage uses: one that derives a balance, and one that records a cash withdrawal as a single statement, a transaction row and two postings. In the terminal, Hassan withdraws fifty pounds inside a transaction. Then a savepoint, a named point to return to, and a second withdrawal from an account that does not exist. The foreign key refuses it, and the prompt shows an exclamation mark: the whole transaction has failed, and the server will accept nothing more. Rollback to savepoint undoes only the failed part. Commit, and Hassan's fifty pounds stand, while the failed withdrawal never happened at all.

How can one session change a row while another reads it, without either waiting? PostgreSQL's answer is multi-version concurrency control, MVCC: an update never overwrites a row in place. It writes a new version, and each version carries hidden columns saying which transactions may see it. Xmin is the transaction that created the version. Xmax is the transaction that replaced or deleted it, zero if none. Ctid is where the version physically sits: a page and a slot. Here is Grace Lin's row: version at page zero, slot three, xmax zero, no phone. Inside a transaction, the team gives her a phone number. Selecting the row again shows a different ctid, slot nineteen, with a new xmin: the updating transaction. That is a new version. The old one is still on disk, and every other session, right now, keeps reading it, because the new version's transaction has not committed. Then rollback. Grace's row is back at slot three, with no phone, and its xmax now names a transaction that never committed, so everyone ignores it. Nothing was undone in place; the server simply forgot the new version. Two things follow. Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. And dead versions pile up until a process called vacuum reclaims their space, which is why vacuum exists, and why the performance stage starts with it.

Now two sessions at once, side by side, each row of this frame one moment in time. Two officers have each been asked to raise Hassan's overdraft limit by one hundred pounds. Both begin a transaction. Officer A reads the limit: zero. Officer B reads the limit: zero. Each plans the same arithmetic in their head: zero plus one hundred. A writes one hundred. B writes one hundred too, and B's update does not return. It waits, because A's update holds a lock on that row until A finishes. A commits. B's update immediately goes through, and B commits. Then A reads the limit again: one hundred pounds, not two hundred. One raise has vanished. Nothing failed, no error appeared, and each officer did exactly what they meant to. B simply overwrote A's work with a value computed from a stale read. This is a lost update, the same failure as the spreadsheet at the very start of the course, and the incident report's double withdrawal is its close cousin. There are two standard fixes. Let the database do the arithmetic, set the limit to the limit plus one hundred, so the second update starts from the committed value. Or lock the row when reading it, so the second officer has to wait before even reading. The next sections show both of these at work.

Isolation levels decide which interferences a database prevents. PostgreSQL's default, read committed, shows each statement the latest committed data, and it prevents neither the lost update nor the next problem, write skew. Chloe and Marcus hold a joint account, with two thousand three hundred and three forty-five in it and a two hundred and fifty pound overdraft. At two ATMs at once, each tries to withdraw one thousand three hundred. Both sessions start serializable transactions. Both check the balance and see two thousand three hundred and three forty-five, so each withdrawal looks fine on its own. Both insert their withdrawal, and neither blocks the other, because they insert different rows. Together they would take the account to minus two hundred and ninety-six fifty, past the limit. A commits. When B tries to commit, the server refuses: could not serialize access due to read-write dependencies. At serializable, PostgreSQL tracks what each transaction read, and B's decision rested on a balance that A's commit made false. B's withdrawal never happened, and the account holds one thousand and three forty-five. The table on the right summarises the three levels in PostgreSQL. The price of serializable is that some transactions are refused and must be retried, with SQLSTATE four zero zero zero one, which the last section turns into a design.

The second fix for the lost update is to lock what you read. Select for update reads rows and locks them until the transaction ends, so nobody else can change them, or lock them, in the meantime. The two officers try again, raising Hassan's limit, which the lost update left at one hundred. Both begin. A selects the limit for update and gets one hundred, and now A holds the row. B runs the same select for update, and it does not return: B is waiting for A's lock. The right-hand diagram is the whole of blocking: one session holds, the other waits. A adds one hundred and commits, which releases the lock. B's select returns at that moment, and it returns two hundred, A's committed value, not the stale one hundred B would have read earlier. B adds one hundred and commits, and the limit is three hundred. Both raises counted. Notice that B did not fail; it waited. That is the trade a lock makes: correctness, paid for in waiting, and waiting is what users experience as a slow bank. Long transactions holding locks are a common cause of production slowdowns, which is why the advice is to lock late, commit early, and never wait for a human while holding a lock. The pg locks view shows which session holds what, and who is waiting for whom.

Locks bring their own failure. Olivia sends money to Hassan at the same moment as Hassan sends money to Olivia. Each transfer locks the account it takes money from, then the account it pays into. Session A locks Olivia's account, one zero one one. Session B locks Hassan's, one zero one two. Now A asks for one zero one two, and waits for B. Then B asks for one zero one one, and waits for A. Each is waiting for the other, and neither can ever proceed: a deadlock. PostgreSQL does not let this run for ever. When a session has waited for deadlock timeout, one second here, the server checks the graph of who waits for whom, and if it finds a cycle, it aborts one of the transactions. Here the check found the cycle in session B, the one whose wait closed it, and B received deadlock detected. Its transaction failed, so its commit became a rollback. A's wait ended at once, and A committed. No data was corrupted, but one customer's transfer failed and would have to be retried. The real fix is not detection but prevention: an order. If every transfer locks the lower account ID first, both transfers here would queue on account one zero one one, the second would simply wait, and a deadlock could not form.

Everything in this stage, combined into one function the bank's app will call for every transfer. First, the file adds a request ID column to transactions, unique: every transfer request from the app carries its own ID. Then the transfer function. Step one locks both accounts, always in account ID order, so two transfers can never deadlock. Step two checks the balance plus the overdraft limit, and it does so after locking, so the balance cannot change between the check and the payment. If there is not enough money, it raises an error, and the whole transaction is refused. Step three inserts the transaction with its request ID, and both postings. In the terminal, request seven seven eight one moves twenty-five pounds from Olivia to Hassan, and returns its transaction ID. Then the app sends the same request again, as an app does when a network connection drops before the answer arrives. The unique request ID refuses it: the transfer happened once. And this is the answer to the incident report. The customer's five hundred pounds left twice because a retried request was treated as a new one. Request seven seven eight two asks Tom's account for a thousand pounds, and is refused: four hundred and four fifty available. Retries are now safe by design: on a serialization failure, the app simply sends the same request again.

Site reliability reports that the statement page takes four seconds. Performance work starts with rules, not indexes. The query must be correct first; speeding up a wrong answer helps nobody. The data must be shaped like production, because a plan on twelve rows says nothing about twelve million. So the team builds a performance schema: thirty thousand postings across three hundred accounts and a hundred days, generated by arithmetic rather than at random, so every replay builds exactly the same rows. Vacuum analyze then gives the planner fresh statistics about them. Now the statement page's query: account forty-two's postings from April onwards, in date order. Explain shows how the server plans to run it, as a tree read from the bottom up. At the bottom, a sequential scan: read every row of the table, and keep only those for account forty-two from April. Above it, a sort by date. For a page that shows ten lines, the server reads all thirty thousand postings. That is the baseline. The last rule is to change one thing at a time and measure again, so that every improvement in this stage comes with its evidence, and none of it is guessed. Timings are never quoted here, only plan shapes and row counts, because those repeat.

Explain shows a plan. Explain analyze runs the query for real and reports what each step actually did. The file turns off the parts that vary from run to run, timings, cache state and cost estimates, and keeps the counts. The sort returned ten rows. The sequential scan also returned ten rows, but look at the line under it: rows removed by filter, twenty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety. To find ten rows, the server read and threw away almost thirty thousand. That number is the cost of this query, and it grows with the table, which is why the page got slower as the bank grew. The second query shows where the planner's beliefs come from. Pg class records, for every table, the estimated number of rows and the number of eight-kilobyte pages: thirty thousand rows on one hundred and ninety-two pages. These figures, and the statistics analyze gathered about each column's values, are what the planner uses to choose between plans. When they are stale, after a big load or a mass delete, the planner can choose badly with complete confidence. Comparing estimated rows with actual rows in explain analyze is the first check whenever a query is slow. Here they agree, so the plan is honest. It is simply doing far too much work.

An index is a separate structure that lets the server find rows without reading the whole table. PostgreSQL's default index is a B-tree: a balanced tree of pages, with keys kept in sorted order. Searching starts at the root page, which holds the first key of each page below it, so the search knows which page to go down to. This index is small, about twenty-seven pages, so below its root are the leaves themselves; a very large table adds a few branch levels in between. Leaves hold every key in order, each with the address of its row in the table. Account forty-two's hundred entries sit together in the leaf, because the keys are sorted. Then the server fetches those hundred rows from the table. A tree like this stays only a few levels deep even for billions of rows, so finding a key costs a handful of page reads at any size. The team creates an index on account ID and runs the same explain analyze. The plan has changed: a bitmap index scan finds account forty-two's hundred rows, a bitmap heap scan fetches them, and only then is the April filter applied, removing ninety. Rows thrown away fall from twenty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety to ninety. A big improvement, but not the end: the index knows the account, not the date.

A composite index covers several columns, in a chosen order. On account ID and then booked on, the index is sorted by account, and within each account by date. So account forty-two's April postings sit side by side in it, already in date order. The order matters: equality columns first, then the range. The same index serves queries on account alone, but a query on the date alone gains little, because dates are scattered across every account. The first explain counts April postings for account forty-two, and the index condition now uses both columns: account forty-two, and booked on from the first of April. The server goes straight to the ten entries it needs. The second query asks the same question differently, with the month extracted from the date equal to four. It looks equivalent, and it returns the same rows, but the plan has changed. The index condition holds only the account; the month test has moved to a filter, checked on every posting of the account. The index is sorted by the date itself, not by a function of it, so once the column is wrapped in a function, the index cannot seek on it any more. The rule: leave indexed columns bare, and compare them with ranges.

The statement page reads three columns: account, date and amount. The index already holds the first two. A covering index carries extra columns as well, written with include. They are not searched by, only stored, so the index alone can answer the query. The team rebuilds the composite index with amount included, and vacuums, which marks the table's pages all-visible. Now the plan is a single node, an index only scan, and heap fetches are zero: the server never touched the table at all. That is as little work as the page can be done with. It is not free, and the second query shows the bill. Every index is a second copy of part of the table, which must be kept up to date. The composite index alone is nine hundred and thirty-six kilobytes, against a table of one and a half megabytes. Every insert into postings now writes the row, and an entry in each of three indexes, and every update to an indexed column does the same. On a bank's busiest table, each index is a tax on every payment. One way to lower it is a partial index, built with a where clause, which indexes only the rows a query needs, such as unsettled payments. The discipline is to add the indexes queries prove they need, and drop the ones nobody uses.

Some questions are expensive however they are indexed: finance's dashboard wants totals for every day, over the whole table. A materialized view stores a query's result, unlike a view, which stores only the query. The file creates one for daily totals: postings per day and their net amount, a hundred rows, computed once. Reading it is reading a small table, which is fast. The price is freshness. The team inserts a new posting on the tenth of April, then reads the materialized view for that day: three hundred postings, minus ten thousand seven hundred and five fifty. The new posting is not there. The stored result is exactly as fresh as the last time it was computed. Refresh materialized view recomputes it, and concurrently means readers can keep using the old result while the new one is built, which requires a unique index on the view. Read again: three hundred and one postings, minus ten thousand six hundred and five fifty-one. A materialized view is a deliberate trade: speed now, in exchange for answers that are minutes or hours old, and it suits dashboards, not balances. How would the team have found the slow page in production in the first place? With pg stat statements, an extension that ranks every query by total time. Next, audit has a finding.

Audit has a finding: tellers can see every branch's customers. Before go-live, access must be designed as carefully as the tables were. Two words first. Authentication is proving who you are; PostgreSQL decides how in a file called pg h b a dot conf, by user, database and address, and this course describes it rather than changing it. Authorisation is what you may do once connected, and that is grants. Privileges belong to roles. A role can be a user who logs in, or a group of privileges that users are given. An administrator connects as the superuser, and the prompt shows a hash sign instead of a greater-than: a reminder that these commands can do anything. The file creates three roles that do not log in: a Leeds teller, an auditor who may read everything and change nothing, and the bank's application. Usage on the core schema lets each of them see into it. The teller may select customers and accounts; the auditor may select every table. And the DB team may act as each role, to test it, without inheriting its privileges. Then the matrix: the server itself is asked, through has table privilege, what each role may do to each table. The app has nothing at all, yet. The auditor reads everything and writes nothing. The teller reads customers and accounts, but not postings.

Least privilege means every role gets exactly what its job needs, and nothing more. Start with the ledger. History must not be editable, by anyone, by accident. So the DB team revokes update, delete and truncate on postings from itself, the owner. An owner can revoke its own privileges, and the database then holds the team to it. Transactions lose delete and truncate.
