Update stays on transactions for a reason the team found the hard way during testing: each posting's foreign key locks the transaction row it points to, and taking that lock requires the update privilege. Revoke it, and no posting could ever be inserted again. Now the app. Rather than letting it write to the ledger, the team gives it one door: the transfer function from the concurrency stage, now marked security definer, so it runs with its owner's rights, with a fixed search path so nobody can slip a lookalike function in front of it. Execute is revoked from public and granted to the app alone. The tests: the team itself tries to update a posting, and is refused. Acting as the app, an insert into postings is refused too. But the app may read balances through the view: Olivia's account, two thousand two hundred and seventy-three ninety-five. The app can move money only the one way that is guaranteed correct.

Now audit's finding itself. A Leeds teller should see Leeds accounts only, and should not see customers' full phone numbers. Two tools, for two kinds of restriction. A view restricts columns: customer directory shows each customer's name and only the last four digits of their phone, and the teller's direct select on customers is revoked, so the directory is the only way in. The view runs with its owner's rights, so the teller can read it without being able to read the table underneath. Row-level security, a PostgreSQL feature, restricts rows. Enabled on accounts, it hides every row from a restricted role unless a policy allows it. The policy for the Leeds teller allows rows where the branch code is LDS; a second policy lets the auditor see everything. Owners bypass policies, so the team's own work is unaffected. Then the team acts as the teller. Counting every account returns nine, and every one of them is in Leeds; the other branches simply do not exist from where the teller sits. The directory returns Amelia, Daniel and Grace, with phones masked, and Grace's empty because she never gave one. And selecting phone numbers from customers directly is refused: permission denied. The finding is closed, by the database rather than by every application remembering to filter.

The most famous database attack needs no privileges at all, only careless code. The app has a search box for payment references. Suppose a user types this: x, a quote, or, quote x quote equals quote x. If the app builds its query by pasting the input into the SQL text, the quote in the input ends the string early, and the rest becomes SQL. The first query does exactly that, building the statement with format and percent s, and running it with backslash gexec. The search returns forty transactions, every one in the table, because the condition became reference equals x, or x equals x, which is always true. With a different input, the same flaw could read other customers' data or delete it. The second query uses percent L instead, which quotes the input as a literal, so the quote in the input is escaped, and the search finds nothing, which is the correct answer. The third way is the right default. A prepared statement has a placeholder, dollar one, and the input is sent separately, as a value. Whatever the user types, it can never become part of the SQL, and again the answer is zero. Every application driver offers parameters; use them for values, always. And when SQL needs a name, a table or a column, which a parameter cannot be, use format with percent I.

Go-live. Here is one ordinary moment in the bank's day, and every layer it passes through. Aisha pays Daniel forty pounds from the bank's app. The app connects as syndica app, and the only thing it may do with money is execute the transfer function, so it calls it, with request ID req nine thousand and one. The function, running as its owner, locks both accounts in account ID order, so a simultaneous transfer cannot deadlock it, and checks Aisha's balance after locking. The keys and references from the build stage make sure both accounts exist. It writes one transaction and two postings, minus forty for Aisha and plus forty for Daniel, which sum to zero, as double entry demands. The request ID means that if the app's connection drops and it retries, the money moves once. Then the app reads balances through the view from the combine stage, derived from postings at that moment: Aisha has five hundred and twenty-seven pounds, Daniel nine hundred and seventy-seven forty. And when the app tries to write a posting directly, the database refuses. None of this depended on the application getting things right. The rules live in the database, where every program that will ever touch the bank's money has to obey them. That is what the DB team built.

That is the course. Starting from an empty server, Syndica Bank's DB team designed a schema whose keys, references and rules refuse bad data; built a double-entry ledger whose balances are always derived and never stored; answered finance's questions with joins, windows and recursion; changed data safely, with reversals, merge and an audit trail; made money movements correct under concurrency, with locks, isolation and idempotent requests; and measured, indexed and secured it all. Every result shown was produced by a real PostgreSQL eighteen server, replayed from one continuous database. Some subjects were deliberately left for later, because each is a field of its own. Running a database in production: changing a schema while it is under load, backups and point-in-time recovery, replication to standby servers, and monitoring. Other database engines: the SQL in this course is portable, and the parts marked as PostgreSQL's are where MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle differ, so those are the places to check. And analytics at scale, where warehouses and engines like Spark apply the same ideas, grain, joins and windows, to billions of rows. Watching a database being built is a start; building one, and seeing your own designs fail and recover, is how the understanding becomes yours.
